THE JOURNAL / Creativity

Make something only you can make.

A fresh perspective starts with the things that make you, you. A field guide to finding your creative voice.

Words by APPICS Journal2 min read

Chapters

  1. Follow what keeps pulling you back.
  2. Make the small version first.
  3. Let the conversation change the work.

There is a moment before every idea becomes something real. Before the first photograph, the first note, the first line. It is the moment when you decide that your perspective is worth sharing. Start there.

Follow what keeps pulling you back.

Your creative voice rarely arrives fully formed. It grows out of the music you replay, the colours you notice, the places you return to, and the questions you cannot leave alone. Collect those things. A folder of references, a few voice notes, or a page of sketches can tell you more than a perfectly written plan.

Look for connections rather than a signature style. What does a favourite photograph have in common with the track you have been listening to? Perhaps it is a feeling, a rhythm, or an unexpected contrast. That connection is a useful starting point.

Make the small version first.

Give yourself one clear constraint: one image, a thirty-second sound, a single scene. A smaller canvas makes it easier to experiment without turning every decision into a statement about who you are. Finish a version, step back, and notice what feels alive.

Your perspective does not have to look like anyone else’s to belong.

Let the conversation change the work.

Share the process as well as the result. Ask a specific question instead of asking whether something is good. Which detail stays with people? Where do they want to look next? Feedback becomes useful when it opens a direction rather than closes one.

Then make another version. A creative practice is built through returning, noticing, and trying again. You do not need to have everything figured out before you begin. You just need something you want to explore.
